_comment: The misconceptions Cambridge names for Stage 4, from the 'Common misconceptions' table in each topic of the Teacher's Resource 4 (Baxter & Dilley) - the same CUP series as Stages 1-3. 26 of the book's 28 topics carry a table; 6.4 Switches and 6.5 Changing the number of components carry none, which is Cambridge's own choice and not an extraction failure. 30 rows were printed across the 26 tables; see _excluded for the one fold. Three other Stage 4 books were supplied and none could contribute: the Hodder Teacher's Guide 4 and Learner's Book 4 have no misconception tables and no 'Look what I can do!' blocks at all (a different series), and neither they nor the CUP Workbook 4 carry a glossary - so unlike Stages 1-3 there is no Cambridge word list behind this grade's vocabulary work, and its self-check claims are written from the 0097 Stage 4 objective statements rather than from Cambridge's own wording.
source: Cambridge Primary Science Teacher's Resource 4 (Baxter & Dilley), Common misconceptions, topics 1.1-6.3
_minimumCovered: Raised to the measured value when the depth pass lands; coverage is a number that only goes up.

_excluded._comment: Printed in a Stage 4 table and deliberately NOT a separate entry here.
duplicate rows folded into one entry: 5.6 'The Sun moves across the sky' is the same misconception as 5.5 'The Sun moves across the sky every day and this is what causes day and night', listed in two consecutive topics with different How to identify / How to overcome text -> one entry, 5.5-m1
_excluded._scoped_rather_than_excluded: 4.4's row ('animals have always been the same as we see them today') is answered at the level Cambridge itself sets for it: its own text says 'Learners do not need to know about this at Stage 4 and they will learn about adaptations, evolution and inheritance later on, but it is a good idea to prepare them for what is to come.' So the entry teaches that animals change very slowly over a very long time, and stops there. 6.1-m1 is scoped the same way: Cambridge mentions free electrons in the teacher's note, and the answerable Stage 4 idea is that the cell PUSHES electricity that is already in the wire rather than making it.

misconceptions.misconception: Bones are not living.
misconceptions.overcome: Your bones are bigger than they were when you were a baby, so they have grown - and growth is a life process. Bones are living parts of you, and a broken one mends itself.

misconceptions.misconception: A skeleton is only there to hold the body up.
misconceptions.overcome: Holding you up is one job of three. It also PROTECTS the soft parts - the skull round the brain, the ribs round the heart and lungs - and it lets you MOVE, because muscles pull on bones.

misconceptions.misconception: Muscles work by pushing as well as pulling.
misconceptions.overcome: A muscle can only PULL. That is why they come in pairs: one pulls the bone one way, and its partner pulls it back.

misconceptions.misconception: An animal with a shell must be an invertebrate.
misconceptions.overcome: A tortoise has a shell AND a backbone inside it, so it is a vertebrate. The shell tells you nothing; look for the backbone.

misconceptions.misconception: An animal with no legs must be an invertebrate.
misconceptions.overcome: A snake has no legs and a long backbone with hundreds of bones in it, so it is a vertebrate. Legs tell you nothing; look for the backbone.

misconceptions.misconception: Plants do not get diseases.
misconceptions.overcome: Plants catch diseases just as people and animals do, from the same sorts of germs. A rusty orange spotting on wheat leaves is a plant disease that can spoil a whole field.

misconceptions.misconception: Energy is a substance - a thing you could hold.
misconceptions.overcome: You cannot hold energy or put it in a jar. Things HAVE energy, and you see what it does - movement, heat, light, sound - but it is not made of stuff.

misconceptions.misconception: Energy gets created when something moves or burns.
misconceptions.overcome: All energy comes from somewhere else. The energy in a kicked ball came from the person kicking it, and theirs came from their food.

misconceptions.misconception: Things use energy up, or run out of it.
misconceptions.overcome: It spreads out instead. When a fire goes out its heat has moved into the room and the air around it - too thinly spread to feel, but not gone.

misconceptions.misconception: Energy is lost or destroyed when it is transferred.
misconceptions.overcome: It changes form. A ball rolling off a table turns its movement energy into the sound you hear, a tiny bit of warmth in the floor, and movement passed into the floor itself.

misconceptions.misconception: A food-chain arrow just means 'eats'.
misconceptions.overcome: It shows which way the ENERGY travels. Living things eat to get energy, so the arrow follows the energy from the thing eaten to the eater.

misconceptions.misconception: There is air in the gaps between the particles in a solid or a liquid.
misconceptions.overcome: Air is made of particles too, and they are far too big to fit in those gaps. In a solid or a liquid the particles are touching, and there is nothing at all in between.

misconceptions.topicTitle: How do solids and liquids behave?
misconceptions.misconception: Every liquid has water in it.
misconceptions.overcome: Cooking oil, syrup and shampoo are liquids with no water in them. Anything that flows and can be poured is a liquid - some just pour more slowly than others.

misconceptions.misconception: Heating something always turns it into a new substance.
misconceptions.overcome: Melted chocolate still tastes of chocolate, and it sets back into chocolate. Melting changes the FORM, not the substance.

misconceptions.misconception: Mixing two substances is a chemical reaction.
misconceptions.overcome: Mix flour and sugar, or sand and water, and you can separate them again by sieving or filtering - so nothing new was made. A reaction makes a new substance you cannot get back.

misconceptions.misconception: The Earth is solid rock all the way through, like its surface.
misconceptions.overcome: Only the thin crust is the rock we walk on. Below it the mantle is hot rock that can move slowly, and the core at the middle is metal - the outer part of it liquid.

misconceptions.misconception: Every volcano is a cone-shaped mountain.
misconceptions.overcome: The Hawaiian volcanoes pour out very runny lava that spreads out flat and wide, making a broad gentle dome rather than a cone. The shape depends on the lava.

misconceptions.misconception: An earthquake and a tsunami are two completely separate events.
misconceptions.overcome: A tsunami is caused BY an earthquake or a volcanic eruption under the sea. The sea floor jolts, and that pushes a huge wave across the ocean.

misconceptions.misconception: Animals have always looked the way they do now.
misconceptions.overcome: Animals do change, but very slowly - over hundreds of thousands of years - so that they suit the place they live. A polar bear and a brown bear are close relatives, and only one of them ended up white.

misconceptions.misconception: We see because light comes out of our eyes and travels to the object.
misconceptions.overcome: Shut a coin in a dark box and you see nothing, however hard you look. Light has to come FROM a source, bounce off the coin, and go INTO your eye.

misconceptions.misconception: Light is everywhere, so it can turn corners.
misconceptions.overcome: Light only travels in straight lines. That is why you cannot see round a corner, and why a torch beam is straight - and why anything in the way makes a shadow.

misconceptions.misconception: Light only reflects off mirrors.
misconceptions.overcome: You can see yourself in still clear water, in a window and in a polished spoon. Light bounces off everything; a mirror is simply the best at it.

misconceptions.misconception: The Earth makes its own light.
misconceptions.overcome: A photograph from space shows HALF the Earth lit and half dark. If it made its own light the whole of it would glow. The Sun is a star and makes light; the Earth is a planet and only reflects it.

misconceptions.misconception: The Sun travels across the sky, and that is what makes day and night.
misconceptions.overcome: The Earth spins once every 24 hours. You are the one moving, so the Sun only SEEMS to cross the sky - which is also why your shadow moves and changes length through the day.

misconceptions.misconception: The cell makes the electricity, which then flows round the circuit.
misconceptions.overcome: The electricity is already inside the copper wire. The cell PUSHES it round - it is the push that the cell provides, not the electricity itself.

misconceptions.misconception: Electricity can only come from the mains.
misconceptions.overcome: A circuit with a cell in it lights a lamp with nothing plugged into a wall. The electricity is in the circuit itself.

misconceptions.misconception: The wire can stop at the lamp - it does not need to go back to the cell.
misconceptions.overcome: There has to be a path all the way from one end of the cell to the other, or the cell has no loop to push the electricity round and the lamp stays dark.

misconceptions.misconception: Tap water is pure, because it is clean and safe to drink.
misconceptions.overcome: Safe to drink is not the same as pure. Tap water has other substances dissolved in it, which is exactly why it conducts electricity - and why water and electricity together are dangerous.

misconceptions.topicTitle: Using conductors and insulators in electrical appliances
misconceptions.misconception: The electricity in a classroom circuit is the same as the electricity at home.
misconceptions.overcome: A cell gives a small, safe push. The mains gives a push hundreds of times bigger, which is why it can kill you and why a cell cannot.
